rows.description: A teammate sees a junior's work presented by someone else and quietly names the real author in the meeting. Small acts of fairness change the culture.
An employee keeps dated records, shares progress in writing, and raises the matter calmly with the person first, and with a manager or HR if it repeats. Facts and calm work better than accusations.
A person negotiating a salary or deal may keep a bottom line private and argue firmly, which is fair. Inventing a rival offer or hiding known defects crosses into lying.
A person is told the offer expires now, or that others would kill for this job, and feels pushed to accept. Asking for time and written terms is a fair response to pressure.
A mature negotiator explains their needs truthfully, asks what matters to the other side, and looks for terms that work for both. Deals built on truth are easier to keep over time.
An employee fudges a number or expense, thinking I will fix it next month or everyone does it. The mind calls it borrowing, and the first step makes later ones easier.
A person under targets, debt or fear of failure finds a gap in controls and gives themselves reasons such as the company can afford it. Most who commit fraud once saw themselves as basically honest.
graph_context: related concepts: rationalisation, fear of failure

rows.description: A team member notices repeated odd adjustments, a boss who resists audits, or a peer living beyond their means. Small doubts deserve to be raised through proper channels early.
A person who has taken the first wrong step can stop, correct the record and speak to a trusted senior or legal adviser. Coming forward early costs much less than being found out later.
An employee who has seen wrongdoing weighs loyalty to colleagues against harm to others and their own job. Doubt, fear and duty coexist, and speaking is a serious personal risk.
